title: Bitwidth fallback harness and attention shim for mixed-precision streaming
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build a lightweight runtime harness that makes per-request and per-head decisions between INT8 and FP8 execution paths with a minimal dequant/requant surface. The goal is to reduce end-to-end decode latency and token cost by opportunistically staying in lower-bitwidth kernels while guaranteeing numerical stability for attention and KV cache reuse.
background: We observed that attempting a single global precision (INT8 or FP8) leaves tail workloads either over-costly or with higher numerical failure modes. Prior tickets focused on kernel arbitration and dequant amortization, but we still see 8-12% latency variance on streaming decode for mixed workloads. This task aims to add a runtime shim that can gracefully fallback at fine granularity to avoid expensive blanket dequant/requant operations.
proposed_solution:
Introduce a 'bitwidth fallback harness' in the serving runtime that contains:
1) a small head-grain gating table driven by telemetry (per-model, per-layer heuristics),
2) an attention shim that can forward to INT8 or FP8 attention kernels with zero-copy when possible,
3) staged dequant bypass: allow downstream compute to operate on cached KV in native quantized format and only trigger dequant if cross-layer numerical drift exceeds thresholds.
The harness exposes a narrow API to the scheduler: resolve_bitwidth(request_context) and attach_shim(node_handle).
tradeoffs_considered:
- Aggressive INT8-first policy reduces cost and latency but increases the likelihood of overflow or accuracy drift; mitigated with short-term fallbacks.
- Per-head gating increases scheduling complexity and memory metadata (small), but reduces unnecessary dequant for multi-head attention.
- Conservative global fallback is simpler but loses most benefits of hybrid execution.
- Adding instrumentation increases runtime overhead; we limit telemetry to sampled requests initially.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (week 1): Add gating table data structures and a lightweight decision function with feature hooks (sequence length, token position, recent numeric anomalies).
Phase 2 (week 2): Implement attention shim that routes to existing INT8 and FP8 kernels. Ensure zero-copy KV pointer compatibility between kernels where ABI permits.
Phase 3 (week 3): Implement staged dequant bypass rules and a small emulated drift detector (stable across 5 recent tokens) to trigger fallback.
Phase 4 (week 4): Add telemetry, end-to-end benchmarks, and canary rollout in runtime-1.20 canary pool.
Phase 5: Post-rollout safety tuning and auto-tuner to seed gating table from historical traces.
test_plan: Unit tests for gating decisions with synthetic numeric traces (overflow, drift, stable).
Microbenchmarks measuring per-token latency for attention path switch (~N runs, CI gated).
Regression tests for KV cache compatibility across INT8/FP8 paths (cache hit/miss scenarios).
Fuzzing long-decode streams to ensure drift detector doesn't oscillate between bitwidths excessively.
Quality evals on held-out prompt set: ensure perplexity/LM loss delta < 0.5% for INT8-first policy after fallback rules applied.
rollout_plan: Canary to 5% of runtime-1.20 canary pool with telemetry sampling enabled.
Monitor latency p50/p95/p99, token-cost delta, and numerical anomaly rate for 24h.
If any of p99 latency increases >5% or anomaly rate >0.1% absolute, automatically revert to conservative global precision policy.
Gradually expand to 25%/50%/100% with auto-tuner seeding at each step.
Post-mortem and knowledge capture after full rollout.
metrics: Primary: p95 decode latency delta vs baseline (target <= -5%).
Safety: numerical anomaly rate (NaN/INF/large residual) per 1M tokens (target <= baseline + 0.05%).
Operational: frequency of bitwidth switches per request (target < 3 per request on avg).
